title: Gnocchi con Burro e Salvia
subtitle: Potato gnocchi with browned butter and crisp sage
excerpt: Gnocchi con burro e salvia is the simplest and most northern Italian way to serve potato gnocchi: tossed in browned butter with sage leaves crisped in the same pan. The nuttiness of the brown butter and the fragrance of the sage are all the dressing this delicate dumpling needs.
sourceNotes: Browned butter and sage (burro e salvia) is the oldest and most traditional pasta sauce in northern Italy, appearing in Italian cookery texts from the Renaissance onward. It is the natural partner for stuffed pasta and potato gnocchi across the whole Alpine north.

content.text: Brown butter (burro nocciola) is made by cooking unsalted butter until the milk solids turn golden and the butter smells of toasted hazelnuts. It takes about 3 minutes over a medium heat and requires attention: it goes from brown to burnt quickly. Add the sage leaves once the butter is golden -- they will crisp in about 30 seconds.
Bake {{potatoes-floury}} potatoes at 200C for 50 to 60 minutes until completely soft. Halve, scoop out the flesh, and rice immediately while hot. Spread to cool for 5 minutes.

Add {{00-flour}} flour, {{eggs}} egg, and {{salt-table}} salt to the riced potato. Mix gently until a soft dough forms. Roll into 2cm-thick ropes, cut into 2cm pieces, and ridge with a fork. Place on a floured tray.
Cook the gnocchi in batches in well-salted boiling water until they float, about 2 minutes. Lift with a slotted spoon and set aside, reserving a cup of the cooking water.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} butter in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook until the butter turns golden brown and smells of hazelnuts, about 3 minutes. Add {{sage}} sage leaves and cook for 30 seconds until crisp. Add the gnocchi and a splash of the cooking water. Toss gently to coat.
Serve in warm bowls with {{parmesan}} Parmesan grated over.

items.symptom: The butter burned before the sage crisped
items.cause: The heat was too high, or the butter was left unattended.
items.fix: Brown butter requires medium heat and constant attention. Watch it until it turns amber, then add the sage immediately and remove from the heat after 30 seconds. Have the sage leaves ready before the butter goes in.

content.text: Burro e salvia is the oldest pasta dressing in the Italian Alpine north. It appears in fourteenth-century Italian cookery texts as a standard sauce for fresh pasta. Before olive oil became widely available in northern Italy, butter was the cooking fat of the region, and sage was plentiful in every garden. The combination is simple and unchanged after seven hundred years.
